title: Tips for Living with Scrupulosity
author: O. Alan Noble
source: You Are Not Your Own (Substack), November 26, 2025
summary: O. Alan Noble, writing from lived experience rather than clinical authority, offers practical guidance for living with scrupulosity—a subtype of OCD in which sufferers obsessively agonize over religious or moral doubts (am I saved? am I forgiven? is God real?) and compulsively seek to resolve an uncertainty that never resolves. His foundational and most counterintuitive claim is that scrupulosity must be treated as OCD, not as genuine spiritual doubt: framing it as theology sends sufferers down rabbit trails trying to answer unanswerable questions, which only feeds the disorder. From that premise he derives four keys—get professional help (specifically evidence-based ERP or I-CBT therapy, not a therapist merely “trained” in OCD), stop seeking reassurance for theological questions, notice and accept intrusive thoughts without engaging them, and ultimately rest in the sovereignty and love of God. He grounds the anti-reassurance advice in Titus 3:9’s warning to avoid foolish controversies, reframing OCD questions as imagination-based “what ifs” rather than here-and-now realities. The acceptance technique he describes—naming a thought, allowing it and its anxiety to exist, and returning to the present rather than fighting it—is presented as a muscle built through practice, undergirded by the one certainty he thinks Christians can hold: not the perfect certitude scrupulosity demands, but confidence in God’s unwavering love.
points: The load-bearing insight is diagnostic reframing—“OCD is OCD is OCD”—treating scrupulosity as special spiritual doubt rather than a mental-health condition is itself part of the condition, and recovery begins by recognizing it as a disorder attacking one’s faith precisely because faith is precious.

Noble is specific about treatment: therapy should be evidence-based ERP or I-CBT, and sufferers should not settle for a therapist merely claiming to be “trained” to treat OCD—while a good therapist will never require an exposure that violates the person’s faith.

The core behavioral prescription is to stop reassurance-seeking, distinguishing one-time “assurance” (asking a pastor once and accepting the answer) from the endless “reassurance” cycle that only strengthens OCD.

He reframes intrusive religious doubts through Titus 3:9 (“avoid foolish controversies”) as imagination-based “what ifs” with no basis in present-tense reality, however urgent they feel in the moment.

The acceptance practice—naming a thought, allowing it and its anxiety to exist, and returning to the present without arguing or playing “tug-of-war”—is framed as a trainable skill, undergirded by trust in God’s sovereignty and the single certainty of his love.
quotes: scrupulosity is a subtype of OCD in which you obsessively agonize over a religious or moral (usually religious) doubt or uncertainty and compulsively try to “resolve” the doubt.
Probably the most important pieces of advice I can give is to treat scrupulosity as OCD, not as some special, spiritual doubt.
But my main point here is that treating scrupulosity as primarily a spiritual question that has to be resolved rather than a mental health condition is a part of the mental health condition.
in Titus 3:9, Paul tells Titus to “avoid foolish controversies,” and I think that’s what OCD questions really are.
Allowing thoughts to just be there and exist without you having to do something to fix them or solve them or figure them out is key to having peace.
Yes, we may have intrusive thoughts that cause us to doubt, but we can be confident that even while we are blown about by doubts, his love never wavers.
